links.outcome: LLM transcription errors: omissions, substitutions, speaker misattribution, medical terminology errors
links.effect: Mean 73 target word errors (3.3%), 51 deletions (2.3%), 19 semantic errors, 8 medical terminology semantic errors; 15 turn-taking errors (7.3% of turns); 48 mis-attributed speaker word errors (2.2%).
links.quote: The LLM produced a mean of 73 ± 26 target word errors (3.3% of all target words), comprising 22 ± 13 substitutions (1.0%) and 51 ± 22 deletions (2.3%).

links.outcome: Transcription errors under higher-fidelity audio versus original audio
links.effect: HFA had fewer target word errors than OFA (23 ± 10, 1.0% vs. 71 ± 25, 3.2%, p = 0.001); semantic errors 10 ± 5 vs. 19 ± 5 (p = 0.011).
links.quote: Semantic word/phrase errors were also significantly lower in HFA recordings (10 ± 5 vs. 19 ± 5, p = 0.011).

links.effect: Medical terminology errors averaged 13 ± 5 per interaction (15% of total word errors), producing 8 ± 4 semantic errors (42% of semantic errors); prompt modification did not help.
links.quote: Medical terminology errors averaged 13 ± 5 incorrect words per interaction, accounting for 15% of total word errors.

links.outcome: Errors in AI-generated transcripts that could enter clinical notes if unreviewed
links.effect: Even modest error rates (3.3% target word errors, 19 semantic errors per interaction) could undermine documentation accuracy; authors caution against autonomous note generation.
links.quote: Our study found modest error rates, yet meaningful errors persisted that could undermine documentation accuracy, confuse clinicians, and cause patient harm.

unlisted_practices: Improving audio recording quality to reduce ambient transcription errors
Prompt modification to alert LLM to expected medical terminology (no effect)

openai.sample_unit: simulated standardized-patient encounters; 6 re-recorded with higher-fidelity audio

links.outcome: Competing transcription tools' word error rates
links.quote: Across the two interactions with a mean 2416 target words, NotebookLM demonstrated substantially lower overall word error rates (96 total word errors; 4.0% of target words) compared with AssemblyAI (252; 10.4%) and Otter.ai (448; 18.5%).

links.effect: Overlapping speech was associated with 16 ± 12 word errors and 8 ± 7 mis-attributed speaker word errors, 19.1% and 16.3% respectively.
links.quote: Out of all total word errors (substitutions, deletions, and insertions) and mis-attributed speaker word errors, 16 ± 12 total word errors and 8 ± 7 mis-attributed speaker word errors were associated with overlapping speech, representing 19.1% of total word errors and 16.3% of mis-attributed speaker word errors.

links.effect: HFA had fewer target word errors than OFA: 23 ± 10, 1.0% vs. 71 ± 25, 3.2%, p = 0.001.
links.quote: Recordings obtained using higher-fidelity audio (HFA) (Supplemental Table 2 ) demonstrated significantly fewer total target word errors than original-fidelity audio (OFA) (23 ± 10, 1.0% vs. 71 ± 25, 3.2%, respectively, p = 0.001), primarily due to reduced deletions (8 ± 5, 0.4% vs. 56 ± 25, 2.5%, respectively, p = 0.001).

links.effect: Mean 73 ± 26 target word errors: 22 ± 13 substitutions, 51 ± 22 deletions, and 9 ± 4 insertions.
links.quote: The LLM produced a mean of 73 ± 26 target word errors (3.3% of all target words), comprising 22 ± 13 substitutions (1.0%) and 51 ± 22 deletions (2.3%).

unlisted_practices: Using higher-fidelity audio recording conditions to reduce LLM transcription errors
Prompting the LLM with expected medical terminology to reduce transcription errors
